digest.definition: Forensic science is the application of science to the purposes of the law, practised differently across jurisdictions; in the UK the aim is ISO accreditation of scene, examination and reporting work
distinctiveFeatures: Forensic science is the application of science to the purposes of the law, practised differently across jurisdictions; in the UK the aim is ISO accreditation of scene, examination and reporting work
The degree is a broad science degree with a strong vocational aim: science and skills used for investigation and justice
Three integrated components make it distinct: scene investigation, laboratory analysis, and the interpretation, evaluation and presentation of evidence
It is multidisciplinary, resting on chemistry, biology, physics, mathematics and statistics, with computer science for digital forensics and law
Scenes and laboratories are read broadly: digital scenes and devices, fire and coroner work, fieldwork, and computer and anthropology laboratories
Practice is regulated and impartial: quality standards, validation, codes of conduct, awareness of bias, and a duty to the court
Professional bodies shape it: the Chartered Society of Forensic Sciences accredits courses and the Forensic Science Regulator sets the codes

subjectSpecific.text: From scene to court, you should work safely and show an understanding of current ISO standards, the law and the Forensic Science Regulator's codes and guidance, impartiality and disclosure included.
From scene to court, you should work safely and show familiarity with professional ethics: respect for the codes of practice and conduct, the standards and rules, and your responsibilities.
From scene to court, you should work safely and show knowledge and understanding of the kinds of cognitive bias, what you lead to (cumulative effects included) and how to reduce them.

From scene to court, you should work safely and show an understanding of approaches such as Case Assessment and Interpretation and the ability to use you in building and delivering a forensic strategy.
Your course should help you work safely and well in a laboratory: assessing risk competently, following written procedures, calibrating where needed and recording methods and results reliably.
Your course should help you use advanced laboratory equipment with confidence where it applies, learn new facilities, and understand the principles behind the instruments.
Your course should help you see why tasks must be done consistently, reproducibly and traceably.

Your course should help you evaluate and critically interpret results by solving problems: finding the relevant scientific principles, planning how to solve you and presenting conclusions as text, tables or graphs.
Your course should help you plan, carry out and report a scientific investigation, analysing the data critically and judging how uncertain it is.
Your course should help you use scientific method on scientific problems, forming a hypothesis and designing experiments to test it.
If you take a master's, your course should also help you work safely and well in a laboratory with little direct supervision.
If you take a master's, your course should also help you plan, design and run new experimental procedures on your own.
If you take a master's, your course should also help you plan, design, conduct and report a research project on your own.
Your course should help you see why standards and codes of conduct are needed and why keeping to you matters.
Your course should help you work well in a team and inside a formal system, following the relevant quality assurance procedures.
Your course should help you record, recover, analyse, evaluate, interpret, preserve and present potential evidence.
Your course should help you build efficient strategies for examining a case.
Your course should help you apply competent procedures that keep evidence intact and its continuity unbroken.
Your course should help you present impartially, in writing and in speech, in ways suited to legal, court and policing settings.
Your course should help you keep to safe working practice, for yourself and others.

Your course should help you appreciate the particular issues, legal framework and practice for digital evidence and trace materials, human and other biological tissue and DNA included, with reference to the Human Tissue Act 2004.
Your course should help you be aware of what modern technology, databases and digital forensics (such as data taken from phones and computers) mean for the field.
Your course should help you appreciate a forensic practitioner's ethical, legal and commercial responsibilities and the quality assurance and validation that professional competence requires.
If you take a master's, your course should also help you gain deep experience of an apt range of forensic methods and take a critical approach to them.
If you take a master's, your course should also help you be open and inventive towards new and emerging forensic procedures and techniques.
If you take a master's, your course should also help you understand the moral and ethical questions forensic practice raises.
You should also understand how serious the results of careless or poor practice can be.
You should also recognise plagiarism as unethical conduct.
You should also know the law on equality and diversity.
You should also know the ethical questions, legal rules and procedures in research, especially with animals or people or with a person's data.

transferable.text: Your course should help you analyse and organise data with ICT, using the software that goes with instruments and working with databases.
If you take a master's, your course should also help you apply and adapt problem-solving to situations that are unfamiliar, complex, poorly defined and open-ended.
Your course should help you build personal and academic resilience by paying attention to your own well-being and that of others.
Your course should help you investigate on your own, drawing on many sources of information and using critical judgement.
Your course should help you communicate complex ideas and information concisely and well, orally and in writing, and interact effectively across many professional settings.
Your course should help you analyse with attention to detail, build logical arguments from incomplete data and use technical language correctly.
Your course should help you use ICT well, including databases, software packages and modern means of communication.
Your course should help you work alone and in a team, and plan, organise and complete work efficiently, conscientiously and on time.
Your course should help you see where further training or new skills would help you improve, and reflect on it.
Your course should help you understand how to put good practice in equality, diversity and inclusion into effect.
If you take a master's, your course should also help you solve problems with self-direction and originality.
If you take a master's, your course should also help you take a self-critical approach to planning, doing and reporting investigations.
If you take a master's, your course should also help you interpret complex technical information with competence and convey it across a wide variety of professional settings.
If you take a master's, your course should also help you keep learning on your own for continuing professional development.
You should also be objective, impartial and honest in every part of your work.
You should also recognise and admit where your knowledge ends.

statements.paraphrase: Interpreting and evaluating evidence means reliable recording, experiment, analysis and interpretation within the case, and clear, impartial written and oral presentation that explains significance and uncertainty; reports and witness statements must be robust, transparent, logical and free of bias, and should separate fact from expert opinion. statements.appliesTo: students of the subject

forPractitioner.text: Students will come to understand, as suits the course, imaging and scene photography and the roles, duties and liabilities of everyone at a scene and how they exchange information, within safe, contamination-aware scene strategy.
